title: Routing and Middleware
summary: Understand the Express middleware pipeline, write a request logger, split routes into Router modules, match Express 5 route patterns and handle 404s and errors in one place.
introduction: Every Express feature is built from one idea: a request passes through an ordered list of functions, and each function either responds or hands over to the next one. Logging, body parsing, authentication, routing and error handling are all just functions in that list. Once you see the pipeline clearly, Express stops being a bag of tricks. In this lesson you write your own middleware, organise routes into modules with `Router`, and add the two handlers every API needs: a JSON 404 and a central error handler.
learningObjectives: Write middleware with (req, res, next) and explain why order matters
Group related routes in an express.Router module
Add a JSON 404 handler and an error-handling middleware with four parameters

blocks.text: A **middleware** is a function with the signature `(req, res, next)`. Express calls the registered functions in the order they were added, and each one decides: send a response and stop, or call `next()` to pass control on. `app.use(fn)` registers a function for every request; `app.get(path, fn)` registers one for a method and path. A request logger is the classic first middleware:

blocks.title: app.js

blocks.text: Request `/api/books` and then `/nope` with curl, and the server's terminal shows one line per request, including the 404 that Express generated itself:

blocks.title: Server terminal (timings vary)
blocks.content:
Listening on http://localhost:3000
GET /api/books -> 200 (3 ms)
GET /nope -> 404 (1 ms)

blocks.text: The logger listens for the response's `'finish'` event, so it can report the final status code and the time taken, then calls `next()` immediately so the request continues down the pipeline. Middleware can also attach data for later handlers: an authentication middleware typically sets `req.user` and calls `next()`, or responds with `401` and stops.

blocks.title: Forgetting next()
blocks.text: A middleware that neither responds nor calls `next()` leaves the request hanging forever: Express is waiting for you. The opposite mistake, calling `next()` *after* sending a response, lets later handlers try to respond again and logs `ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT`. Each middleware should do exactly one of the two, and `return next()` makes the intent obvious.

items: Loggers and `express.json()` go first, so every route sees a parsed body.
Routes come next, most specific first: `/api/books/featured` must be registered before `/api/books/:id`, or `featured` is treated as an id.
The 404 handler goes after all routes; it only runs when nothing above responded.
The error handler goes last, so that errors from everything above reach it.

blocks.text: `Router()` creates a mini application with its own routes and middleware. You define routes relative to the router, then mount it under a prefix with `app.use`. One router per resource keeps `app.js` short as the API grows:

blocks.title: routes/books.js
app.js

blocks.code:
curl -s http://localhost:3000/api/books/2
curl -s http://localhost:3000/api/books/9
curl -s http://localhost:3000/api/authors

blocks.text: Inside the router, `/:id` is relative to the mount point, so it matches `/api/books/2`. `req.originalUrl` keeps the full path for logging, while `req.path` inside a router is the part after the prefix. Routers can also have their own `router.use` middleware, which is how you protect only `/api/admin` with an authentication check.

rows: Named wildcard; `req.params.path` holds the rest. The bare `*` of Express 4 no longer works
Braces mark an optional group; replaces the Express 4 `/:id?` syntax
Any number of parameters; each is one segment

blocks.text: An error handler is a middleware with **four** parameters; Express recognises it by the arity, so `next` must stay in the signature even if you do not use it. Any route that throws, or calls `next(err)`, skips the remaining routes and lands here. Since Express 5 this includes rejected promises from `async` handlers, which Express 4 silently dropped:

blocks.title: An async route that fails
curl -s http://localhost:3000/api/boom, and the server terminal
blocks.content:
{"error":"Something went wrong"}

Error: database down
    at file:///home/ada/bookshelf/app.js:8:9
    ... (stack shortened)

blocks.text: The client receives a generic message while the terminal gets the full stack. Never send `err.message` or `err.stack` to clients in production: they can reveal file paths, queries and library versions. If you need distinguishable errors, give them a `status` property (`err.status = 404`) and let the handler use `err.status ?? 500`.

rows: Parses JSON bodies into `req.body` when `Content-Type` is `application/json`; limit 100 kB by default

blocks.title: Third-party middleware
blocks.text: Most cross-cutting needs already exist as packages that follow the same `(req, res, next)` contract: `cors` for cross-origin requests from browsers, `helmet` for security headers, `morgan` for logging, `express-rate-limit` for throttling. Add them with `app.use` in the same order rules as your own middleware.

questions.question: How does Express tell an error-handling middleware apart from a normal one?
questions.explanation: Express checks the function's length: a middleware declared with four parameters (err, req, res, next) is treated as an error handler.
options: It has four parameters: `(err, req, res, next)`
It must be the first middleware

questions.question: In Express 5, an error thrown inside an `async` route handler is passed to the error-handling middleware automatically.
questions.explanation: Express 5 catches rejected promises returned by handlers and calls next(err) for you; in Express 4 such a request would hang unless you caught the error yourself.
